extracted.intended_audience: novelists, critics, and serious readers studying the craft of fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative standards for reading, criticizing, and composing the novel—focusing on form, modes of narration, selection/arrangement, point of view, and the technical uses of scene and narrative. Intended to help critics recreate a book and writers choose disciplined methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read aright / constructive reading
rubrics_metrics.description: “The beginning of criticism is to read aright, in other words to get into touch with the book as nearly as may be.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical reading is an active recreation: the reader must deliberately reconstruct the book's form rather than passively enjoying episodes or characters. Reading 'aright' means standing at a distance from the material enough to perceive and assemble it into a coherent book.

rubrics_metrics.name: A book has a certain form
rubrics_metrics.description: “A BOOK has a certain form… that a book is a thing to which a shape is ascribable, good or bad.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge novels as shaped objects: assess whether their form is coherent, proportioned, and appropriate to the subject. Recognize the tension between a novel as a passage of time and as a completed, welded mass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on how novels are made
rubrics_metrics.description: “How they are made is the only question I shall ask.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism should concentrate on the novelist’s technical choices—selection, arrangement, point of view, modes of narration—rather than merely on broad praise or biographical notes. The craft (the making) is the primary evaluative axis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection and arrangement
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist’s essential task is to select fragments of life and arrange them into an ordered, artistic whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the author’s choices of what to include and how to order incidents serve the subject. Poor selection/arrangement will make the subject seem imperfectly expressed; good selection yields a compact, meaningful book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form, design, and composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Form, design, composition are aspects of the novel analogous to other arts, though applied loosely in literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider proportion, balance, and the distribution of emphasis. Though fiction may be more forgiving than other arts, composition still affects a novel’s power; assess whether the novel obeys or abandons these compositional principles to good effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of the dramatic incident (the scene)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The dramatic incident, the scene, properly so called—this comes first in importance, beyond doubt.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dramatized scenes deliver the sharpest effects and should be the chief resource for emphasizing key moments. Use scenes to clinch effects that have been prepared by other means rather than to do all the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations and economy of the scene
rubrics_metrics.description: A scene “displays the whole of the time and space it occupies” and is therefore expensive in time/space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that scenes cannot cover more than they render; they act vividly but slowly. Authors should prepare scenes in advance and use them sparingly for maximal effect. Critics should note when scenes are wasted or misapplied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pictorial (picture) narrative
rubrics_metrics.description: The pictorial or ‘picture’ mode “travels over periods and expanses… its office is to pile up an accumulated impression.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pictorial narration to cover time and space economically, to accumulate impression and background material. Beware its thinness; the novelist can convert that thinness into strength by dramatizing the mind that mirrors events (i.e., centering impressions in consciousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Panoramic / broad sweep
rubrics_metrics.description: Large, panoramic novels (e.g., War and Peace) present vast masses of life and detail across time and many persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the novelist successfully handles scale—holding character detail while providing the sweep—and whether a clear subject or organizing idea anchors the panorama. Judge whether the form conveys a coherent subject or dissolves into profusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view selection and consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: “The point of view gives only a general indication… the point of view from which it is to be approached.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and maintain an appropriate point of view (authorial omniscience, limited consciousness, etc.). The POV determines permissible instruments and the overall look of the story; mismatches between POV and treatment weaken the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Modes of narration / authorial voice
rubrics_metrics.description: Identifies different narrative voices and licences (e.g., the minstrel’s licence—the author plainly telling the story—versus more limited, mediated voices).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether an author’s chosen voice is appropriate and disciplined. The ‘minstrel’ (easy omniscient) is allowable only if it genuinely serves the story; otherwise it is the ‘easy way’ that curtails deeper possibilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and survivability
rubrics_metrics.description: Powerful character-drawing leaves durable impressions—people like Clarissa, Anna, Emma remain as positive facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether characters are made intelligible and vivid through selection, incident, and scene. Strong characterization is a primary test of a novel’s imaginative power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and coherence (the novel as a welded mass)
rubrics_metrics.description: The reader should, by deliberate recreation, find “a complete, coherent, appraisable book” remaining in the mind—“a welded mass.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the parts cohere into a single form expressing the subject. Critical recreation should aim to recreate such unity and then judge whether the form succeeds in expressing its materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Matching instruments to stages of the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide when to use dramatic scene, pictorial narration, panoramic treatment, or other devices at different stages of development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A novelist must have a working theory of the relative uses of different means and apply them where their peculiar strength is required (e.g., use scene to crown effects, picture to accumulate impression). Critics should ask whether these choices are appropriate at each moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Convert method limitations into artistic strengths
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a method seems weak (e.g., pictorial thinness), the author may assert and emphasize that quality and thus convert it into a new kind of strength.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate how an author uses the constraints of a chosen mode (e.g., indirect pictorial report) to create distinctive effects—such as dramatizing the mind that reflects events—to turn an apparent disability into power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discipline and avoidance of the easy way
rubrics_metrics.description: “The easy way is no way at all; the only way is that by which the most is made of the story… by a choice and disciplined method.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor deliberate, disciplined methods over casual or facile narration. Criticism should penalize methods that avoid the craft’s demands, and praise authors who make rigorous, appropriate technical choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical literacy in narrative forms
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic and novelist should recognize and name the various forms of narrative (dramatic, pictorial, panoramic, centered consciousness) and their properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop precise critical terminology and awareness of narrative modes; practical criticism requires understanding these forms in order to perceive their demands and qualities and to use them consciously in composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reader as recreator / critic as craftsman
rubrics_metrics.description: “The reader of a novel—by which I mean the critical reader—is himself a novelist; he is the maker of a book… the critic must overtake [the author] at his work and see how the book was made.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics must actively reconstruct the book’s form and workmanship. The value of criticism lies in studying the craft—following the process of selection, arrangement, and technique—and thereby understanding or judging the novel more precisely.
